use: General independent band calculation, without using its alternating premise to equate signs.
actual_read_body:
1.1 Suppose first that there is at least one crossing. Take small disjoint crossing neighborhoods and thin strips along the finitely many projection edges. Each region of the chosen color has a disk core in the complement of these strips; connectedness makes the projection a cellular graph on the sphere, so shrinking its open disk regions gives exactly these disk cores. At every crossing join the two appropriate disk cores by a narrow band with one half-twist; choose its direction so that its boundary strands have the diagram's prescribed overpass and underpass. The neighborhoods are disjoint, so the resulting surface is embedded. Its boundary is the usual height realization of $D$. Collapsing each disk to a vertex and each band to its core retracts $F$ onto the Tait graph $G$. This graph is connected by [F2], so $F$ is connected and has a supplied finite disk-and-band presentation. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Measure the signed half-twist of a band relative to the planar framing of its two disk ends; call this incidence sign $\epsilon_e$. This is the unoriented crossing incidence, not the oriented link crossing sign. At two crossings joined by a projection edge, alternation changes which branch is over, while the chosen-color sector changes sides along that edge. The two changes cancel in the half-twist chart, giving the same incidence sign at the two crossings. Since the projection graph is connected, every band has one common sign $\epsilon$. Reversing the chosen orientation of a graph edge reverses its cycle coefficient, without changing this incidence sign. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 We compute the normal pairing in the disk-and-band presentation. After clearing rational denominators, represent a cycle by finitely many oriented parallel strands through each band, joined by arcs in the vertex disks; any extraneous arc pairs can be canceled inside those disks. The signed number of strands through band $e$ is its graph coefficient $a_e$. Normal transfer gives two local pushoffs of each strand, exchanged at a one-sided passage. In an untwisted planar disk the contributions of the two normal sides to the mixed-crossing count cancel. In a band with a signed half-turn, each ordered pair of an original strand and a transferred strand contributes $\epsilon_e$ to the total pairing: one normal side passes from one side of the original strand to the other during the half-turn, and the other normal side makes the complementary passage; the two mixed crossings have the same incidence sign, and the linking count is half their signed sum. Reversing either strand orientation reverses the corresponding contribution. Consequently the contribution of that band is $\epsilon_e(\sum_i s_i)(\sum_j s_j)=\epsilon_e a_e^2$, where $s_i=\pm1$ are the strand orientations. This is also a direct computation with the half-twisted strip $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v\cos(\pi u),v\sin(\pi u))$, reversing the half-turn for the other sign. The strips' end collars are included in this count; crossings of joining arcs in the planar disks cancel between the two normal sides. Linking here can be computed by the signed mixed-crossing count because a finite oriented smoothing of the first curve gives spanning disks and crossing bands, whose intersections with the second curve give that count. This finite construction uses the supplied drawing and does not use a link-diagram invariance theorem. Summing over all bands and restoring rational coefficients gives $\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)=\sum_e\epsilon_e a_e^2$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 By [F3] and the retraction in step 1.1, a homology class has a unique graph cycle vector. Thus $q(a)=\epsilon\sum_e a_e^2$ is a well-defined quadratic form on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, and step 3.1 proves the required normal-transfer formula for every representative. If $a\ne0$, some edge coefficient is nonzero, so $\sum_ea_e^2>0$. Therefore $q$ is positive definite if $\epsilon=1$ and negative definite if $\epsilon=-1$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If the connected diagram has no crossings, it is a single circle. Either complementary disk is an embedded connected spanning disk with $H_1=0$. Every cycle in that disk bounds there and has zero linking with its normal transfer, so the zero-dimensional form has the asserted formula and definiteness. This also covers the zero-dimensional cycle space of a Tait tree in the preceding case. [given, F1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

use: Actual smooth finite handle reduction, disk/circle extension and tree absorption; not inferred from its Statement alone.
actual_read_body:
1.1 All local selection in the compact constructions below is finite. In a $C^2$ chart choose nested coordinate balls and compose a Euclidean smooth bump with the chart; extension by zero gives a $C^2$ bump with support in that chart. Finite compact-core covers and normalization by the positive finite sum give $C^2$ partitions. In a smooth ambient manifold the same construction gives smooth bumps and partitions near a compact set. For a compact abstract $C^2$ surface $S$, choose finitely many such charts $x_i$ and bumps $b_i$ whose positive sets cover $S$. The map $J=(b_i,b_ix_i)_i$, extending each block by zero, is a $C^2$ embedding into a finite-dimensional Euclidean space: equality of the $b_i$ blocks and any positive $b_i$ recovers equality of $x_i$, hence of the points. If $dJ(v)=0$, then $db_i(v)=0$ and $b_i dx_i(v)=0$ for a positive block, hence $v=0$. A continuous injective map from compact $S$ to a Hausdorff space has continuous inverse on its image; the local inverse in chart projections is $C^2$ by [F1]. Half-space charts give the same argument at the boundary. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 First treat a closed cooriented embedded hypersurface $S$ in a smooth three-manifold. In finitely many ambient neighborhoods take $C^2$ defining functions $F_i$, zero precisely on $S$ there, with their differentials positive on the chosen common normal side. Multiply by an ambient smooth partition $\rho_i$ whose sum is one near $S$ and put $F=\sum_i\rho_iF_i$. On $S$, $dF=\sum_i\rho_i dF_i$, because $F_i=0$ kills every term $F_i d\rho_i$; this differential is nonzero and positively normal. Local implicit uniqueness and a finite shrinking therefore give a neighborhood of $S$ on which $F^{-1}(0)=S$. Positive local smooth transverse vectors, shrunk so they remain positive, glue by smooth nonnegative weights to a smooth field $V$ with $dF(V)>0$ near $S$. Finite coordinate convolutions and an ambient smooth partition, using [F2], give a smooth $G$ arbitrarily close to $F$ in $C^2$ on a compact smaller neighborhood. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Write $\Phi_t$ for the smooth flow of $V$. Compactness gives a uniform short flow strip on which $dF(V)>c>0$; the map $(x,t)\mapsto\Phi_t(x)$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism on a smaller strip about $S$. Its differential is invertible on the zero section; if no uniform injective strip existed, coincident points in successively thinner strips would have convergent base points, their limits would coincide, and local injectivity at that point would contradict the coincidences. For $G$ sufficiently close, $dG(V)>c/2$ and $G$ has opposite signs at the strip ends. Thus $G(\Phi_t(x))=0$ has a unique root $t=\tau(x)$, $C^2$ by [F1]. The map $x\mapsto\Phi_{\tau(x)}(x)$ identifies $S$ with the smooth level in that strip. Its $C^2$ inverse is obtained by the unique root of $F=0$ on the same flow orbit. A time cutoff extends the displacement to a $C^2$ ambient diffeomorphism supported in the strip: in these coordinates use $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t+\eta(t)\tau(x))$; choosing the approximation small makes $1+\eta'(t)\tau(x)>0$. [F1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The abstract embedding in step 1.1 can have higher codimension; a scalar defining function is not asserted for it. Here is the needed finite replacement. A $C^2$ embedded surface is locally a graph $v=h(z)$ over a fixed two-plane by [F1]. On a compact graph patch replace $h$ by a smooth $h'$ arbitrarily close in $C^2$, and use the ambient map $(z,v)\mapsto(z,v+\eta(z,v)(h'(z)-h(z)))$, with a smooth compactly supported $\eta$ equal to one near the compact graph core. If the difference is sufficiently small in $C^1$, this is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism: its difference from the identity has derivative norm less than one, which proves injectivity by the mean-value estimate, and the local inverse is $C^2$; compact support gives surjectivity. The moved surface is a smooth graph near that core. To preserve already smoothed compact cores $K$, take $h'=h$ near their projections wherever the patch meets $K$. Such projections have an open neighborhood where $h$ is smooth. A smooth cutoff $\mu$, supported in that neighborhood and one near the relevant compact projections, gives $h'=\mu h+(1-\mu)h_\epsilon$, which is smooth and $C^2$ close to $h$. Cut the ambient support away from any other protected cores. The displacement is then the identity near $K$. [step 3.1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

5.1 Choose compact chart cores covering the original surface. Carry those cores and the remaining graph neighborhoods along each displacement. Apply step 4.1 successively to the finitely many cores, with the union of the earlier moved cores protected. Compactness allows finite refinements into graph patches and arbitrarily small displacements so that all needed graph projections remain regular. After the last patch the image is smooth near every core, hence everywhere. For boundary charts, extend the local graph $C^2$ across its half-plane boundary before convolution; the definition of $C^2$ regularity in a boundary chart supplies precisely such local extensions. This initially smooths the underlying surface graph, leaving a regular $C^2$ boundary curve in those smooth graph coordinates. Apply the same finite graph displacement argument, now to one-dimensional boundary graphs within these smooth surface coordinates, relative to previously smoothed boundary cores. Its coordinate displacements are $C^2$, have support in these patches, and smooth the boundary; every boundary core then has a smooth half-space chart. This proves the abstract assertion without an atlas-smoothing theorem. [F1, F2, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 For an actual cooriented surface region with boundary, one can retain the normal-root construction. Extend its local surface graphs across the regular boundary and apply step 2.1 on a finite neighborhood of the region; at the boundary the extensions agree on the interior side, which is all that is needed for the root projection of the region itself. The moved region lies in smooth local surface graphs and has $C^2$ boundary. Alternatively step 5.1 provides an unambiguous finite ambient construction there. On the smooth underlying surface near the boundary, take a $C^2$ signed boundary defining function $H$ using finitely many boundary graph charts and smooth weights; its inward differential is nonzero. Smooth it to $H'$ and take a smooth inward-transverse surface field $W$. The equations $H'(\Psi_t(y))=0$, with $y$ on the old boundary, give a $C^2$ boundary displacement with inverse obtained from $H=0$. Extend it with a cutoff in its flow collar exactly as in step 3.1. This maps the region to a smooth-boundary region. A compact intrinsic leaf subsurface has embedded ambient inclusion: the leaf inclusion is an injective immersion, and its restriction to a compact intrinsic subsurface is a homeomorphism onto its image by compactness and Hausdorffness. The above finite construction therefore applies; other, possibly dense, parts of that leaf are not part of this carrier. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Let $\psi:S^1\to S^1$ be an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism. Its increasing $C^2$ lift $a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $a(\theta+2\pi)=a(\theta)+2\pi$ and $a'>0$. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\beta$ zero near $r=0$ and one near $r=1$. In polar coordinates put $E(r,\theta)=(r,\theta+\beta(r)(a(\theta)-\theta))$. Periodicity makes this well-defined, and its angular derivative $1-\beta(r)+\beta(r)a'(\theta)$ is positive. Thus each circle map is bijective; [F1] gives a $C^2$ inverse on the annulus, and $E$ is the identity near the origin. This is a $C^2$ disk diffeomorphism restricting to $\psi$, with product collar expression near the boundary. For an orientation-reversing map first compose with the fixed reflection of the disk. The same formula is smooth for smooth data. [step 6.1, F1, construct]

8.1 We give the smooth normal-form argument explicitly. Apply [F4] to the smoothed surface with empty incoming face and boundary as outgoing face; use both faces empty in the closed case. Obtain finitely many disks (zero-handles), rectangles (one-handles) and capping disks (two-handles), with all zeros before ones before twos. Before forming the graph, transport any attaching windows on earlier rectangles back to zero-disk boundary arcs: along a rectangle side use its product collar, move the finite windows in order to its endpoint collar, and continue onto the zero-disk boundary, shrinking windows to leave disjoint gaps. For an increasing interval map $f$ fixed at the endpoints, the collar map $(s,t)\mapsto((1-\alpha(t))s+\alpha(t)f(s),t)$ has positive first derivative; successive such maps give each transport and carry the affected band with it. Induction over the finitely many bands gives a presentation with every band attached to disjoint intervals of zero-disks. Its core is then an edge between the zero-disks. The resulting graph is connected when the surface is: each capping disk attaches along a connected circle and cannot join two components. Choose a finite spanning tree. The union of its disks and bands is diffeomorphic to a disk, by successive leaf disk-and-band absorptions described next. Every other attaching interval is transported in these absorptions, rather than discarded. [step 7.1, F4, construct]

9.1 For the absorption move, two disks joined along a single band are a disk after rounding their four corners: straighten the two attaching intervals in boundary collar coordinates, rescale the band's product coordinates to a rectangle, and identify the resulting union with a planar rounded disk-and-rectangle model. Its boundary is parametrized by the successive arcs and the two sides of the rectangle; a collar of that boundary and radial coordinates on a smaller interior disk give the usual disk parametrization. More explicitly one may straighten the disks into end caps of the rectangle and choose the rounded union to be a convex stadium, hence star-shaped about its midpoint; its radial boundary function is positive and smooth, and radial rescaling, cut off to a constant linear rescaling near the center, identifies it with a round disk. Boundary arc parametrizations are transported by increasing interval maps. If attaching windows of other bands lie on the absorbed disk, they remain disjoint ordered intervals on the new disk boundary. To put them in prescribed positions choose an increasing boundary map with the prescribed maps on those finitely many disjoint intervals; on the complementary intervals interpolate positive derivatives with the required integral. On a boundary rectangle $(s,t)$ extend its isotopy by $(s,t)\mapsto((1-\alpha(t))s+\alpha(t)f(s),t)$, with the interval endpoints fixed and $\alpha$ zero at the inner edge. Its Jacobian in the $s$ direction is positive. Composing finitely many such collar maps transports all attaching windows and their band coordinates. This is the explicit surface handle slide/straightening needed for each tree contraction; it invokes no higher-dimensional handle-slide theorem. [step 8.1, construct]

10.1 After primal contractions there is one zero-disk. View the same presentation upside down: a two-disk is a dual zero-disk, a rectangle is a dual rectangle with its factors interchanged, and the zero-disk is a dual capping disk. The dual graph is connected by the same connectedness argument. A dual spanning tree and the absorptions of step 9.1 leave one dual zero-disk, hence one original two-disk. Transport later attachments at every contraction by the same rectangle collar maps. These operations are actual diffeomorphisms of the entire surface: the disk-plus-band replacements agree on the boundary collars used to attach the rest. Each primal contraction decreases $h_0,h_1$ by one, and each dual contraction decreases $h_1,h_2$ by one. If $\chi=0$, [F4] now gives $0=1-h_1+1$, hence precisely two remaining bands. This calculation concerns the actual Morse handles, regardless of how many cells were present in any original topological cellulation. [F4, step 8.1, step 9.1, construct]

11.1 Orientability forbids a twisted band. The first untwisted band on the remaining disk gives an annulus: straighten its two windows by the collar maps in step 9.1; the standard disk with that rectangle is the planar annulus. The second band must join its two boundary circles. Indeed, attachment to intervals on the same boundary circle of an oriented annulus increases the number of boundary components to three, whereas joining the two circles leaves one, and the single final two-disk can cap only one circle. Straighten the two windows on the different annulus circles and extend their boundary maps over disjoint collars. An interval attaching map has no additional twist once the surface orientation is fixed; positive changes of its longitudinal parameter extend across the rectangle by the positive-derivative interpolation in step 9.1. Thus this is the standard annulus with one joining band, a once-punctured torus. Its remaining boundary is a circle; a circle attaching diffeomorphism extends over the final disk by step 7.1. Capping therefore gives the standard torus. Composing with the carrier diffeomorphism proves the $C^2$ torus assertion. [F4, step 5.1, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, construct]

12.1 For a smooth region homeomorphic to a disk, cap its outgoing boundary with an auxiliary disk and mark that disk as an exterior dual vertex. A smooth circle parametrization needed for the cap is obtained by ordering finitely many regular curve charts around the circle and choosing a positive smooth speed on their overlaps. First contract the primal tree as above. The capped surface's dual graph is connected; choose a spanning tree rooted at the marked exterior vertex. Successively absorb the other dual disks towards that root using step 9.1. In original coordinates this deletes an internal two-disk together with a band; the exterior disk is not deleted, and its boundary collar is transported, so removing it at the end gives a diffeomorphism of the original region. There remain one zero-disk, no two-disks and $h_1$ bands. Its Euler characteristic is one, since it is homeomorphic to a disk, so [F4] gives $1=1-h_1$, hence $h_1=0$. The region is therefore a smooth disk, by an actual composition of disk/band collar moves. Pulling back by step 5.1 gives a $C^2$ parametrization of the original disk region; composing with the extension in step 7.1 realizes any prescribed boundary parametrization. [step 11.1, F4, step 5.1, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, construct]

13.1 For completeness, an oriented compact annulus has a disk-and-band normal form by the same moves. Cap both boundary circles with marked exterior disks, contract the primal tree, and contract a dual forest rooted at those exterior disks (one root for each component of the forest). Every internal dual disk is absorbed into a root, so in the original annulus no internal two-disk remains. There is one zero-disk and, by $\chi=0$, one band. Orientability and the two boundary components make this the standard untwisted annulus. For two disjoint regular disks in a $C^2$ sphere, first smooth the sphere and then both marked boundary curves by the boundary moves in step 6.1, transporting the disks. Choose a common signed transverse-flow collar of each resulting smooth boundary curve. All disk-and-band moves can use these supplied collars: their interval maps extend as product maps on smaller collars and are cut off farther inside by the positive-derivative interpolation of step 9.1. For these disks their complement is connected with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero: paths can be rerouted around each removed disk along its boundary collar, and capping these two boundary circles recovers the sphere. The preceding normal form identifies this complement with an annulus. Given compatible boundary parametrizations, their increasing angle lifts $a_0,a_1$ extend across it by $a_t=(1-\lambda(t))a_0+\lambda(t)a_1$, with $\lambda$ constant near both ends; the angular derivative is positive. Parametrize the two disks by step 12.1 with those same collars, and use the constant-end interpolation on the annulus with the common signed collar coordinate. The maps on the two sides thus have identical product expressions on a whole seam neighborhood, so gluing is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism. This gives the simultaneous sphere diffeomorphism and prescribed windows. The scalar approximation assertion is [F2], after extending the function by a cutoff equal to one near its compact set and convolving. [F2, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, step 12.1, construct]

14.1 Let $K=u(D^2)$, compact in the intrinsic topology. Choose finitely many precompact leaf charts with $C^2$ bumps $b_i$ positive on $K$, as in step 1.1. Their sum $b$ has compact support in $L$ and a positive minimum on $K$. Take a regular value $c$ strictly between zero and that minimum: cover the compact support by finitely many charts and apply [F3], so the finite union of bad value sets is null and cannot fill this interval. Then $P=\{b\ge c\}$ is a compact intrinsic $C^2$ subsurface with regular boundary and contains $K$ in its interior. Step 5.1 supplies a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $q:P\to P'$ with $P'$ smooth. Glue two copies of $P'$ along a smooth boundary collar to obtain its compact smooth double $Q$; collars can be read in the finite smooth boundary charts, gluing their inward fields by a finite smooth partition and taking their smooth flow. Thus $q(K)$ lies in the interior of the designated copy of $P'$ in the boundaryless smooth carrier $Q$. [step 13.1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 5.1, construct]

15.1 By [F5] smoothly embed $Q$ into $\mathbb R^N$, writing $j$ for the embedding, and take a smooth retraction $R$ from a tubular neighborhood onto $j(Q)$. Let $v=jqu$. This is continuous on the disk and $C^2$ on the given open collar. Extend it continuously across the disk boundary by its boundary values constant on short radial rays, and multiply outside a larger disk by a continuous compact-support cutoff. Euclidean convolution gives smooth maps $v_\epsilon$ uniformly approaching $v$ on $D^2$ by [F2]. Choose a smooth scalar cutoff $\gamma$ equal to zero near the specified smaller collar and equal to one off a slightly larger collar whose closure still lies in the original $C^2$ collar. Set $w_\epsilon=v+\gamma(v_\epsilon-v)$. Where $\gamma\ne1$, the original $v$ is $C^2$; where $v$ is only continuous, $\gamma=1$ on a neighborhood and $w_\epsilon=v_\epsilon$. Thus $w_\epsilon$ is $C^2$ everywhere and equals $v$ near the smaller collar. [F2, F5, step 14.1, construct]

16.1 The compact set $v(D^2)$ is inside the tubular domain and inside $j(\operatorname{int}P')$. By continuity of $R$ and compactness, sufficiently small uniform perturbations and their entire straight segments from $v$ remain in the tubular domain and retract into $j(\operatorname{int}P')$. Define $u_\epsilon=q^{-1}j^{-1}R(w_\epsilon)$, using $j^{-1}$ on that copy. It is $C^2$, agrees with $u$ near the prescribed smaller collar, and converges uniformly to $u$. The formula $q^{-1}j^{-1}R((1-s)v+sw_\epsilon)$ gives a continuous homotopy fixed there. Uniform convergence in any compatible metric follows from uniform continuity of $q^{-1}j^{-1}R$ near this compact image; no regularity or injectivity of $u$ was used away from its collar. [F5, step 14.1, step 15.1, construct]

17.1 The finite constructions prove the carrier, normal-form and relative approximation assertions. All selections particular to these compact carriers are finite. Countable choice is inherited only from the convolution, smooth-flow, Morse/handle, smooth-embedding and tubular suppliers; no arbitrary-index Axiom of Choice or general $C^2$ atlas-smoothing result is used. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 6.1, step 11.1, step 12.1, step 16.1] ∎

use: Exact angular formula restricted to the actual smooth strips; no ambient TOP-to-smooth upgrade.
actual_read_body:
1.1 Use [F1] and shrink its fixed normal cylinder to $|x|\le1$, $\sqrt{y^2+z^2}\le\delta$. Strict radius monotonicity and compactness give one point on each $F_1$ half at every sufficiently small normal radius $r>0$, for each $x\in[-1,1]$. They depend smoothly on $x,r$ for positive radius. The function $Z(x,t)$ is nonzero for $-1<x<1$ and $t\ne0$ in this cylinder, because otherwise there would be an extra intersection with $F_0$ away from $A$. Its linear coefficient $Z_t(x,0)$ is also nonzero there, by transversality along the open common arc. Reverse the $t$ coordinate if needed to make this coefficient positive. The two connected half-strips then have $Z>0$ for $t>0$ and $Z<0$ for $t<0$. Thus their positive-radius angles have unique lifts $\alpha_+(x,r)\in(0,\pi)$ and $\alpha_-(x,r)\in(\pi,2\pi)$ for interior $x$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 These lifts extend continuously to $r=0$ and the two end faces. Indeed $(Y,Z)=t\,v(x,t)$ with smooth nonzero $v$ on the closed strip; the normalized positive and negative half directions therefore extend uniformly as their signed $t$ tends to zero. At each end $v=(\sigma_\pm,0)$, so the positive-half angle is exactly zero or $\pi$, and the negative-half angle is respectively $\pi$ or $2\pi$. By [F2], $\sigma_-\ne\sigma_+$: the first surface has the same positive $y$ direction at its two boundary lines, so opposite end matchings mean precisely opposite signs for the second surface. Choose $\theta(x)=\pi(x+1)/2$ when $\sigma_-=1$, and $\theta(x)=\pi(1-x)/2$ otherwise. Its endpoint angles coincide with those of $\alpha_+$, and $\theta+\pi$ with those of $\alpha_-$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct]

3.1 Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\mu(r)$ equal to one near zero and zero near $\delta$. For $0\le u\le1$ and $-1<x<1$, prescribe target angles $\gamma_+=(1-u\mu)\alpha_++u\mu\theta$ and $\gamma_-=(1-u\mu)\alpha_-+u\mu(\theta+\pi)$. They remain respectively in $(0,\pi)$ and $(\pi,2\pi)$. On each normal circle use the increasing piecewise-affine angle map fixing $0,\pi,2\pi$ and taking $\alpha_\pm$ to $\gamma_\pm$, affine on each of the four intervening intervals. Its slopes are positive, so it and its inverse are circle homeomorphisms. The formulas depend continuously on $u,x,r$ as long as the breakpoints are distinct. At an end face they converge uniformly to the identity: the maximum angular displacement on the four affine intervals is bounded by $\max(|\gamma_+-\alpha_+|,|\gamma_--\alpha_-|)$, which tends to zero by step 2.1, uniformly in $r,u$. The inverses have the same uniform displacement bound. Define the angle maps to be the identity on the two end faces. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Preserve $x$ and normal radius and apply those angle maps for $r>0$; fix the axis at $r=0$. This gives a homeomorphism of the closed cylinder for each $u$, continuously in time, with the inverse furnished by the inverse angle maps. Continuity at the axis needs no angular limit: normal radius is unchanged. It is the identity at $u=0$, near the cylinder's radial boundary, and on both end faces by step 3.1, so it extends by the identity outside the cylinder to an ambient topological isotopy. It fixes the whole local first surface pointwise because the angles zero and $\pi$ are fixed, and fixes the local link on the end lines for the same reason. The chart was chosen to contain no other portions of the link or the first surface, so their remaining portions are fixed too. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 At $u=1$ and $r$ so small that $\mu(r)=1$, the two $F_1$ half-strip angles are exactly $\theta(x)$ and $\theta(x)+\pi$. Their unique points at each normal radius thus fill exactly the signed-radius ruled strip in the Statement. The first surface remains its original flat strip and their boundary remains the literal two original end lines. Every map was an ambient homeomorphism fixing the axis, so no point identifications or extra intersections were introduced. This proves the relative local normal form, while retaining explicitly the topological regularity of the isotopy at its possible nonsmooth loci. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

use: Graph-convolution fiber map; seam-fixed center adjustment is proved directly in the new consumer.
actual_read_body:
1.1 At a seam choose its unit tangent and the ambient orientation. Project the inward transverse tangents of the two half-sheets to the normal plane and normalize to unit vectors $a(s),b(s)$, retaining the supplied labeling. They vary smoothly and are distinct. The normal field $e_x=(a-b)/|a-b|$ and its positive quarter-turn $e_y$ give a smooth normal frame along the entire seam, also around a circle. The two inward rays have respectively positive and negative $e_x$ component, since $a\cdot(a-b)=1-a\cdot b>0$ and $b\cdot(a-b)=a\cdot b-1<0$. Use a smooth ambient metric and its normal exponential map in this frame. By [F1] and compactness it gives one tubular coordinate system $(s,x,y)$ around the seam, with a short extension at arc ends. The projection of each half-sheet onto $(s,x)$ has invertible differential up to its boundary. Hence, after a uniform shrinking, their union is exactly a graph $y=f(s,x)$, smooth jointly in $s,x$ on each side of zero, continuous with $f(s,0)=0$, and with no other surface portions in the tube. The finite disjoint seam tubes can be made disjoint. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The nonsmooth locus is a compact subset of the seam interiors: the smooth locus is open in $S$, the seams are compact, and the arc ends and $K$ have protected smooth neighborhoods. Choose smaller seam tubes and a smooth cutoff $\mu(s)$ equal to one near every nonsmooth seam point and zero near the protected set and arc ends. Its transition regions along the seam are chosen where $S$ is already smooth. This is possible by finite interval charts and scalar bumps on the finitely many parameter circles or intervals. Shrink the tube widths so the support misses a neighborhood of $K$ and lies in the prescribed neighborhood; away from those parameter intervals no modification is required. There are finite uniform graph widths and slope bounds on the compact support. Choose a horizontal cutoff $\zeta(x)$ equal to one near zero and zero outside a narrower graph strip, and a small positive kernel width $\epsilon$. Let $f^\epsilon$ denote convolution in $x$ and set $g=f+\mu(s)\zeta(x)(f^\epsilon-f)$. By [F2], $f^\epsilon$ is jointly smooth across zero. Near a nonsmooth seam point both cutoffs equal one, so $g=f^\epsilon$. Where $\mu$ changes, $f$ is smooth in a neighborhood of that seam point; where $\zeta$ changes, $x\ne0$ and $f$ is smooth. It follows that $g$ is smooth everywhere on the modified graph. Take $\epsilon$ smaller if necessary so the graph error $\Delta=g-f$ has arbitrarily small uniform norm. [step 1.1, F2, construct]

3.1 Choose a fixed vertical cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$. Take a small vertical width $a>0$, choose the horizontal strip so that $|f|<a/4$ there, and ensure $\|\chi'\|_\infty|\Delta|/a<1/2$. Define $T_t(s,x,y)=(s,x,y+t\chi((y-f(s,x))/a)\Delta(s,x))$, $0\le t\le1$, on the tube. Its derivative in $y$ is greater than $1/2$, so each vertical fiber map is an increasing homeomorphism equal to the identity near the fiber ends. The horizontal and parameter cutoffs make it the identity near the other tube boundaries as well. The fiber inverses are continuous jointly in $t,s,x,y$, by the same lower slope bound and monotonicity. Extend by the identity outside the tube. This is an ambient topological isotopy, and at $t=1$ it carries the graph of $f$ exactly to the graph of $g$. Its support can be made as small as specified by the choices in step 2.1. The formula requires no differentiability of $f$ at the seam. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, construct, algebra]

4.1 Apply these constructions to the finitely many disjoint seam tubes. Their isotopies have disjoint support and therefore compose to one ambient isotopy, fixed on a neighborhood of $K$. At its endpoint each affected portion is the smooth graph $g$, agrees with the original smooth graph near all support boundaries, and introduces no intersection because it is the image under a homeomorphism. Outside the tubes the surface was smooth from the start. Thus the entire image is a smooth embedded surface, with the stated support and relative properties. Opposite inward rays cause no difficulty: their $e_x$ components still have opposite signs, and the same graph and convolution argument applies. Only coincident rays would invalidate the graph projection, and they were excluded explicitly. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

use: Finite supported perturbation pattern only; new final theorem supplies its own proof and does not perform crosscap normalization.
actual_read_body:
1.1 Choose a small normal push $K_i'$ disjoint from the whole surface $F$. Triangulate its finite disk-and-band presentation and choose arbitrary reference orientations on its finitely many triangles. Their sum modulo two is a fundamental two-chain with boundary the sum of the boundary circles modulo two. Lift that two-chain to an integral chain $C$ in $S^3\setminus K_i'$ by using the chosen triangle orientations, and orient the boundary circles as prescribed in the Statement. Then $\partial C-\sum_j K_j=2z$ for an integral one-chain $z$. Its boundary is zero, because $2\partial z=0$ and singular chain groups have no integer torsion. Applying the linking homomorphism with $K_i'$ from [F1] gives $0=\sum_j\operatorname{lk}(K_i',K_j)+2\operatorname{lk}(K_i',z)$. This use on $z$ is on complement homology and does not require it to be embedded. For $j\ne i$ the small push is homotopic to $K_i$ in the complement of $K_j$. The $i$th term is $f_i(F)$ by symmetry. Reduction modulo two proves the stated parity formula, independently of the orientability of $F$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 A smooth boundary circle has an oriented normal disk bundle with a smooth trivialization. One may construct it on a cut parameter interval using finitely many normal frames, then correct the endpoint rotation by a smooth angle interpolation so that the frames glue; the oriented two-plane rotation group is connected. The normal exponential chart is injective at a sufficiently small uniform radius by [F4] and compactness, as in the normal-transfer construction. In these coordinates a nowhere-zero transverse vector along the circle has an angular lift on the cut interval, whose endpoint difference is $2\pi$ times an integer. Its small pushed curve is a longitude plus that many positive meridians. By [F1] its self-linking is the self-linking of the reference longitude plus this integer. In particular two such fields have the same self-linking precisely when their angular lifts differ by a periodic smooth function. Surface inward conormals and surface normals along an oriented boundary circle differ by a fixed quarter-turn in its oriented normal plane. They therefore have the same integer and the same self-linking. These assertions concern boundary collars only and do not orient the whole surface. [given, F1, F4, construct]

2.1 By step 1.1 the difference $d_i=f_i(F_1)-f_i(F_0)$ is even. If $d_i\ne0$, add $|d_i|/2$ crosscaps of sign $\epsilon=\operatorname{sign}(d_i)$ to that component of $F_0$, using [F2]. Each increases that component's self-linking by $2\epsilon$: the total Euler change is $-2\epsilon$, and the other component self-linkings are unchanged. Such a small separated attachment is available in a boundary chart, placing its Möbius band in a small ball off the surface and joining through a product collar of the chosen boundary arc. After each attachment use the local boundary-link isotopy in [F2] to return the boundary to the original $L$; linking and framings are transported by that isotopy. Use disjoint small boundary neighborhoods for the finitely many required attachments, or successive smaller neighborhoods. Connectedness and the finite disk-and-band presentation are retained. This produces a surface $\widehat F_0$ whose component framings equal those of $F_1$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, construct, algebra]

3.1 Work in disjoint sufficiently short normal tubes of the boundary circles, containing no other parts of either surface than their boundary collars. Choose the tube coordinates adapted to the actual collar of $F_1$, so it is the radial ray of angle zero. Explicitly extend its collar parametrization $c(s,x)$ slightly across $x=0$, and map $(s,x,y)$ to the short ambient normal push by $y$ of $c(s,x)$. The boundary-circle tangent, the inward collar vector and its ambient normal are independent, so [F4] gives this chart at $x=y=0$, and compactness gives a uniform tube. The finite boundary-chart extensions agree on the prescribed collar and can be patched beyond its boundary before shrinking. Thus the whole collar, rather than only its tangent line, is the angle-zero ray. On a short collar of $\widehat F_0$, the base projection to the boundary circle is a coordinate and the normal radius is a strictly increasing inward parameter. This follows at the boundary from the nonzero inward transverse derivative, then uniformly by compactness and [F4]. Thus its collar has coordinates $(s,r,\theta(s,r))$, with its angular direction tending to a smooth angle field at $r=0$. Its relative angular winding is zero by steps 1.2 and 2.1. It therefore has a periodic real angular lift on a sufficiently short collar. First straighten its angle to its limiting field on a smaller radius strip, using an angular interpolation cut off before the outer edge; then interpolate that limiting field to a fixed small angle $\delta\ne0$, again cut off in radius. Throughout these interpolations the base coordinate $s$ and radius $r$ are unchanged, so distinct parameters remain distinct and the collar stays embedded even if the angle varies in $r$. The formulas extend smoothly across $r=0$: they are rotations of the smooth transverse vector by a periodic smooth angle, while the initial straightening error vanishes with $r$. All changes vanish on an outer collar. The final innermost collar is the ray of angle $\delta$ and is disjoint from the angle-zero interior collar of $F_1$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F4, construct]

4.1 Extend the collar embedding isotopies of step 3.1 by the unchanged embedding on the remainder of $\widehat F_0$ and use [F5]. The ambient extension fixes every boundary point because the embedding isotopy fixes it; no claim that this extension fixes the comparison surface is needed. Perform it on the finitely many disjoint boundary tubes. Denote the endpoint by $F_0'$. It still has boundary $L$, retains its component framings by [F3], and misses $F_1$ in a punctured neighborhood of each boundary component. Shrink to a common such neighborhood $U$. The given finite smooth presentation is transported by the isotopies. [step 3.1, F3, F5, F6, construct]

5.1 It remains to make the intersection outside $U$ transverse. In the boundaryless ambient manifold $S^3\setminus L$, the target $F_1\setminus L$ is a closed embedded boundaryless surface. All possible intersections of the two surfaces are contained in a compact region outside a smaller $U$. In finitely many ambient charts covering that region choose three bump-supported vector fields spanning each tangent space on smaller covering charts, with supports away from a still smaller neighborhood of $L$. Compose their short flows with parameters $a_j$, obtaining ambient diffeomorphisms $h_a$ fixed there. At zero parameter the parameter derivatives span the ambient tangent space on every possible intersection. For a sufficiently small parameter ball the same remains true at all intersections, by compactness and continuity; regions outside those covering charts retain their positive separation or are fixed. Thus the evaluation $(x,a)\mapsto h_a(x)$ from the interior of $F_0'$ is transverse to $F_1\setminus L$. Apply [F6] and choose an arbitrarily small good parameter. The path of short flows from zero to it is an ambient isotopy fixed near $L$. Its endpoint $F_0^*$ is transverse to the comparison surface outside $L$ and retains the separated collars. [step 4.1, F5, F6, construct]

6.1 Their interior intersection is now a compact one-dimensional smooth manifold with no boundary: it is transverse away from $L$ and absent in a punctured neighborhood of $L$. Compactness gives a finite cover by connected interval charts, so there are finitely many components. Each component is closed and hence compact, and [F7] makes it a smooth embedded circle. Thus only finitely many interior circles remain. Every crosscap move preserved the corrected signature by [F2], and every subsequent ambient isotopy preserved both its pairing signature and all component self-linkings by [F1] and [F3]. Their finite composition therefore preserves $\operatorname{sign}(B)+e/2$. The component labels and chosen orientations were transported throughout. This proves the claimed normalization while leaving the remaining entire-surface comparison as a separate obligation. [step 2.1, step 5.1, F1, F2, F3, F7, construct] ∎
